A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): whorled (multiple leaves clearly attached at the same node, visible in close-up images)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): clustered (leaves are grouped tightly at the apex of the stem)

B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): simple (each leaf is a single blade without subdivisions)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): N/A
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): N/A
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): N/A

rag_matches.description: Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Adult plants frequent in the forest; seedlings common and recognizable by the large orbicular fimbriate stipules. Flowers in the late rainy season (August to November). The fruits mature within 1 month. Costa Rica to Peru and Brazil. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Colon and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone (Pipeline Road), Veraguas, and Panama (Cerro Jefe). [Paullinia turbacensis] is a tendriled liana; stems terete, ± glabrous, bearing conspicuous brown lenticels; sap at periphery milky, not copious. Leaves trifoliolate; petioles to 14 cm long, with marginal ribs above, glabrate; leaflets broadly elliptic, acuminate or acute at apex, attenuate to rounded at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-12 cm wide (to 23 cm long and 11 cm wide as juveniles), glabrate but with axillary tufts below, subentire to remotely crenate-dentate. Thyrses small, helicoid, to 7 cm long, solitary or clustered at nodes, often on leafless stems near the ground but occurring to 5 m high; flowers white, ca 5 mm long; petals with the scales ca two-thirds as long as petals, yellow-crested, the anterior scales bilobed, their appendages pubescent, the glands white, acute, densely pubescent; staminal cluster equaling petals; filaments densely pubescent; nectar abundant, stored near the large glands; ovary glabrous; styles pubescent. Capsules elliptic to obovate, 2 cm long, red, short-pubescent, the 3 boat-shaped valves broadly spreading to expose seeds; seeds 1-3, black, shiny, less than 1 cm long, covered on the lower half by a fleshy white aril, dangling on a thin funiculus when fully displayed.

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Tree, 4.5-35 m, the young twigs minutely adpressed-pubescent to glabrescent. Leaves with the petiole 0.5-1.2 cm; blade 10-30 X 3.5-12 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, acute to obtuse or (rarely) subtruncate at the base, glabrous on the underside, without domatia or (rarely) with countable trichomes in the axils of the main veins, with (4)5-8 secondary veins on each side. Inflorescences [of Nectandra purpurea] 10-17 cm. Flowers with the tepals (1—)1.2—2(—2.4) mm. Fruits 1-1.5 cm, ellipsoidal; cup ca. 0.3 cm. Very wet and pluvial forest, 0-1550 m; Caribbean [vertical] Cords. of Guanacaste, Triarán and Central (E.B. La Selva), San Carlos and Tortuguero Plains, Low Talamanca, both [vertical] Cord. de Talamanca, [Pacific] vertical, S Coastal Range (Fila Cruces). Flowers [of Nectandra purpurea] May-Sept. [in Nicaragua, Bolivia] and [Venezuela], [in the] Guiana [region], [in] Brazil. (Grayum et al. 8898, MO) Nectandra purpurea is recognized by its leaf blades that dry relatively opaque on the adaxial side, with the secondary veins slightly elevated and interconnected, forming a submarginal vein and by its flowers with the tepals densely covered by brown or yellowish trichomes and (usually) with the staminodes conspicuously elevated. The cupules that dry light brown, ± puberulent, are also distinctive.

Inflorescences with peduncle 0.4-8 cm, [unclear reference], [unclear reference]. Fl. mar.-may., nov.

Tree, 5-30 m; young twigs ferruginous-tomentose. Leaves with petiole 0.8-2 cm, wide, slightly channelled; blade 9.8-32.7 X 3.7-10.5 cm, ovate to oblong or elliptical, rounded to cuneate at the base, acute or acuminate to cuspidate at the apex, generally glabrous on the adaxial surface (sometimes pubescent along the midrib), ± densely ferruginous-tomentose on the abaxial surface with persistent, pedicellate trichomes, with 10-18 secondary veins per side. Inflorescences paniculate, highly branched, up to ca. 18 cm. Flowers brown. Fruits green (but densely ferruginous-pubescent), 1-1.5 X 0.8-1.2 cm, ellipsoidal to globose; seed 0.8-1.2 cm. Very humid forest, 0-900+ m; Caribbean slope. Ranges of Guanacaste, Tilarán and Central, San Carlos and Tortuguero plains, both slopes N of the Talamanca range, Pacific slope, N Coastal Range (near Boruca), P.N. Carara, Puriscal region (P.N. La Cangreja), P.N. Manuel Antonio, Golfo Dulce region. Fl. Jan.-Jun., Sep., Dec. Honduras-Bolivia and Venezuela, Guianas, Brazil.

Locating an individual
Cantarrana, around the station.
Distribution
From Mexico to Brazil. In Costa Rica, widespread in very humid wet forests on both slopes; 0-1,150 m.
Habit
Tree, 10-35 m tall.
Trunk
Cylindrical trunk, with slender, cylindrical, grayish twigs; small stipules attached to the petiole.
Bark
With smooth, grayish bark.
Leaves
Simple, alternate leaves, 2.5-12 x 0.8-5 cm, ovate to oblong, acuminate apex, rounded to cupped base, whitish or grayish on the underside, 5-9 pairs of secondary veins, entire margin; petioles 3-7 mm long.
Flowers
Greenish-yellow flowers, 1.5 mm long, with absent petals and 3-5 stamens. Inflorescences panicles, up to 16 cm long.
Fruits
Fruits drupes, 1.5-1.8 cm long, pear-shaped to ovoid, pink when ripe.
Diagnosis
Distinguished by its clearly bicolored leaves, the underside whitish to grayish and the thin blade with very fine reticulation. Also, by its pear-shaped fruits.
Habitat
Generally observed in forests on rolling terrain.
Phenology
Fruits observed in July.

Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, Colombia, and Venezuela. In Costa Rica, 0-500 m; Caribbean slope, Central and Talamanca mountain ranges, Guatusos plains, San Carlos, and Tortuguero; Pacific slope, Osa Peninsula.

Shrub or tree, 1.5-6 m.

Trees or shrubs, dioecious, with white sap; stipules separate and paired (which leave a partial scar on the twig when the stipules fall). Leaves distichous; blade generally serrated, sometimes entire. Inflorescences solitary or paired, spicate or racemose (in Costa Rica), shortly pedunculated. Flowers sessile or pedicellate, the staminate with the perianth 4-parted, the segments imbricate; stamens 4, the filament straight in the bud; pistillate flowers with the perianth tubular, subentire or 4-lobed; ovary free or adnate to the perianth at the base; style 1 with 2 short stigmatic arms. Fruits drupaceous, completely immersed in the growing fleshy perianth. Vegetatively, Sorocea could be confused with Trophis and even with Batocarpus. From the former genus, Trophis, it differs in that Trophis has long and slender stigmas, while Sorocea has short and thick ones; Batocarpus differs by having syncarpous infructescences.

Locating an individual
Intersection of the Southwest Trail (SSO) with the Hartshorn Trail (SHA).
Distribution
From Mexico to Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Venezuela, and the Antilles. In Costa Rica, 0-1100 m; Both slopes of the Talamanca Mountain Range; Caribbean slope, Central Mountain Range, Plains of the Guatusos and San Carlos; Pacific slope, Central Pacific, Osa Peninsula.
Habit
Tree, 8-612(-40) m.
Leaves
Leaves 13-39 x 6-22 cm, elliptical to elliptic-ovate, 5-veined.
Flowers
Flowers 5(-6-7)-merous; calyx 0.5-1 mm, inconspicuously lobed, the outer teeth about 0.5 mm, subulate; petals 2-2.5 mm, glabrous.
Fruits
Fruits 0.4-0.5 cm.
Diagnosis
Tree plants; young twigs (and petioles and axes of the inflorescences) densely covered with massively dendritic and shortly pediculate trichomes (sometimes simple and longer on the interpetiolar ridge), the underside of the leaves and hypanthium copiously covered with mostly creamy starry-lepidote trichomes; leaves 5-veined, conspicuously discolorous (green on the adaxial side and light brown on the abaxial side), with petioles deeply longitudinally striated; inflorescences panicles with sessile and glomerulate flowers; flowers 5(-6-7)-merous, with the calyx inconspicuously lobed, with glabrous petals, the stamens with slightly anisomorphic anthers and the ovary 3-locular. It is very similar to
M. argentea
, whose twigs are conspicuously laterally angled (completely quadrangular in
M. elata
) and whose leaves have short and strongly revolute bases, forming a sort of domatia on each side of the adaxial apex of the petiole (flattened in
M. elata
).
Habitat
Wet and very wet forest.
Phenology
Flowers observed in September and November. Fruits observed from March to May, in September and November.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins. Panicles stout, bracteated, divaricately branched, terminal; buds depressed-globose; pedicels stout, to 1 cm long; flowers thick, 5-parted, spreading at anthesis, to 4.5 cm diam, white to pink, the lobes often marked with maroon or magenta at base or apex; sepals 2, concave, unequal, persisting in fruit; petals 4-10, broadly oblong, 2-2.5 cm long; androecium of staminate flowers cushion-shaped, ca 1 cm wide and 5 mm high with numerous anthers; pollen white, granular, compressed in round or oval pouches ca 1 mm diam, embedded just beneath the sticky surface of the disk; pistillate flowers similar to staminate but the gynoecium divided into (4)9(15) segments, the petals falling soon after anthesis, the sepals closing. Capsules subglobose, 2.5-3 cm long, dehiscing into 5-9 parts at maturity; valves thick, ± spreading to expose the colorful mass of seeds; seeds numerous, reddish, curved-oblong, ca 5 mm long, embedded in a deeply divided, bright-orange aril. Frequent epiphyte in the forest or on exposed shorelines; epiphytic on rocks or on trees near the edge of the water. Plants are usually supported on tree trunks or large branches but the branches may grow into the top of the canopy. Apparently flowers and fruits sporadically throughout the year. Where plants occur along the shore, the branches usually root at the nodes with the roots hanging in the water. The pollen sacs of the staminate flowers burst under the slightest pressure, and abundant pollen oozes out (sometimes explosively). Several species of small bees, including Trigona spp., have been seen visiting the flowers. The geographical range of Symphonia globulifera extends from Nicaragua to Panama, probably to Colombia. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone, Colon, San Bias, Veraguas, Herrera, Panama, and Darien, from premontane wet forest in Code (El Valle) and Panama (Cerro Campana), and from tropical wet forest in Code (La Mesa) and Panama.

Life Form: Liana 
9. Strychnos panamensis Seem., Bot. Voy. Herald 166 (1854). Holotype: Panama, Seemann s.n. (BM). Illustrated: Blackwell, Ann. Missouri Bot. Gard. 54: 408, t. 5 (1967). By A.E. Brant and G. Davidse. Strychnos hirtiflora (Standl.) Lundell, S. longissima Loes., S. panamensis Seem. var. hirtiflora Standl., S. tabascana Sprague et Sandwith. Lianas, with tendrils, without spines; yellow hairy plants with long, ascending, scattered trichomes, in addition to curved, short trichomes. Leaves with petioles about 5 mm, variably hairy, from sparsely hairy with some scattered ascending trichomes to densely hairy; blades about 9 × 3.5 cm, membranous to slightly coriaceous, shiny on both surfaces when mature, highly variable in size and shape, narrowly elliptical to almost ovate, the base cuneate to rounded, the apex narrowly to broadly acuminate, the adaxial surface hairy on the main veins, the abaxial surface variably appressed hairy, especially on the main veins and scattered and long-ciliate near the base of the mature blades, often sparsely hairy over the entire surface. Inflorescence in a loose terminal cluster, axes and branches thinly hairy with long ascending trichomes. Flowers with calyx lobes about 2 mm, lanceolate, glabrous to densely pilose externally, glabrous internally, long-ciliate; corolla tube about 2 mm, externally glabrous to densely pilose, corolla lobes about 4 mm, curved and reflexed at anthesis, glabrous to densely pilose externally, woolly towards the tip internally, the rest glabrous; style about 2.3 cm, glabrous; anthers about 0.7 mm, rounded at both ends, glabrous, exserted on filaments of about 2 mm. Mature fruits 5-8 cm, globose, smooth, shiny; yellow, the shell 2-3 mm thick; numerous seeds, the testa crustaceous. Beaches, high evergreen forests. Ch (Martínez S. 16283, MO); QR (Chan 6715, MO); B (Brokaw and Schulze 37, MO); G (Lundell 16517, MO); H (Nelson et al. 6567, MO); ES (Sandoval and Sandoval 1012, MO); N (Moreno 25470, MO); CR (Hammel and Grayum 14281, MO); P (Croat 10299, MO). 0-1800 m. (Mexico [Oaxaca, Veracruz], Mesoamerica, Colombia, Venezuela, Guianas, Ecuador, Peru.) We decided to treat Strychnos panamensis and S. tabascana as a single species. Flowers are needed to make the distinction, therefore all sterile and fruiting collections automatically become S. panamensis.

Life Form: Liana

Leaves with petioles about 5 mm, variably hairy, from sparsely hairy with some scattered ascending trichomes to densely hairy; blades about 9 × 3.5 cm, membranous to slightly coriaceous, shiny on both surfaces when mature, highly variable in size and shape, narrowly elliptical to almost ovate, the base cuneate to rounded, the apex narrowly to broadly acuminate, the adaxial surface hairy on the main veins, the abaxial surface variably appressed hairy, especially on the main veins and scattered and long-ciliate near the base of the mature blades, often sparsely hairy over the entire surface. Inflorescence in a loose terminal cluster, axes and branches thinly hairy with long ascending trichomes. Flowers with calyx lobes about 2 mm, lanceolate, glabrous to densely pilose externally, glabrous internally, long-ciliate; corolla tube about 2 mm, externally glabrous to densely pilose, corolla lobes about 4 mm, curved and reflexed at anthesis, glabrous to densely pilose externally, woolly towards the tip internally, the rest glabrous; style about 2.3 cm, glabrous; anthers about 0.7 mm, rounded at both ends, glabrous, exserted on filaments of about 2 mm.
